messages:
jess: Quick follow-up from the kernel-selection RFC — we discovered a few edge cases when the KV cache is paged/blocked and kernels expect contiguous KV per layer. TL;DR: eviction holes + fragmented pages break some attention kernels. Need proposals for compatibility layers.

omar: can you paste a minimal repro or tensor shape that trips it?

jess: Repro is simple: model with long context, KV cache is split into 64KB pages, eviction removes middle pages -> attention kernel expects a contiguous KV buffer per head, so indexing math is wrong. Here's trimmed output from the failing assert: 

```
AssertionError: expected contiguous_kv_stride == cached_stride
cached_stride=256, contiguous_kv_stride=0
```

This happens in the fused rotary-attn kernel when it reads KV with a single stride.

liam: ah yeah. Some of our hand-written CUDA kernels assume a packed layout for performance. When paging we added an indirection table at a higher layer, but we didn't wire the kernels to read via that indirection.

sam: So two options: 1) change kernels to tolerate indirection (slower but correct), or 2) ensure eviction/reassembly always produces contiguous regions before invoking those kernels.

omar: another angle: keep two execution paths — an "indirect" kernel variant that follows per-token pointers, and a "packed" fast path. Router picks based on cache fragmentation metadata. Could be runtime-overhead to choose and maintain both ABI variants though.

jess: agree. We should weigh perf delta vs engineering complexity. Also consider memory pressure patterns: fragmentation will be rare for many workloads (short queries) but common for long-running chat sessions with targeted evictions.

liam: Measurement we ran last week: the indirect variant was ~25-40% slower on microbenchmarks, mostly due to uncoalesced memory loads. But it avoids copies. Reassembly/copying pages into a contiguous buffer costs us ~10-20% and extra bandwidth but gives full-speed kernels.

sam: So copying has an advantage: once contiguous buffer is made, all existing optimized kernels work unchanged (no kernel churn). But it increases transient memory usage and complicates eviction accounting.

jess: I sketched a middle ground: a cheap adapter that maps sparse pages into a small batch-local scratch buffer only for the active sequence window. Steps: detect fragmentation for the batch, if fragmented and the batch size is small, copy only the needed ranges into scratch; otherwise fall back to the indirect kernel. This keeps copy cost bounded.

omar: sounds practical. Need to formalize the heuristics: threshold on number of pages per request, total bytes, and locality (are pages contiguous except a few holes?). Also add a fast path to skip copying if pages already contiguous.

liam: Also watch out for head cache consistency: if we copy into scratch, we must ensure eviction/updates don't race while kernel reads. We either take a read-lock on pages or copy under a snapshot mechanism. Locks add latency. Snapshot via epoch counter + CAS should work.

sam: Implementation plan proposal:
- Add fragmentation metric per model-instance (num_holes, largest_contiguous_run, total_pages)
- Router sets a flag per request whether to use `packed-copy`, `indirect-kernel`, or `fallback-bypass`
- Implement small scratch-copy utility that copies only the per-request layer ranges (aligned to page boundaries)
- Add microbench harness and unit tests that inject holes and assert correctness + perf threshold

jess: + include tracing: tag requests with chosen path and report percent of traffic on each path. We need this telemetry to tune heuristics.

omar: question: eviction policy change? If we bias eviction to avoid creating small isolated holes (prefer evicting contiguous ranges), we reduce fragmentation at the source. Could we implement page-coalescing on free to reduce holes?

liam: coalescing is good, but under steady-state churn we still get interleaving from different sessions. Also coalescing requires background compaction which can be expensive. But a best-effort coalescer that merges adjacent free pages asynchronously is feasible.

sam: we should also think about pointer indirection layer API: currently it's internal. If we expose a read-iterator that kernels can opt into, future kernel devs can write indirection-aware kernels more easily. API needs to be minimal: provide per-layer stride, pointer-to-page, length, and a gather primitive.

jess: OK action items:
1) Omar + Liam to prototype a scratch-copy adapter and an indirect-kernel stub (two PRs).
2) Sam to add fragmentation metrics + tracer tags.
3) Jess to author micro-RFC with heuristics and test plan (include synthetic workloads: long chat, many small requests, burst evict).
4) Add a compaction/coalescer spike to observe cost/benefit.

omar: I'll take the indirect kernel stub and a small perf harness. ETA EOW.

liam: I'll prototype the scratch-copy and the unit tests. + I will add correctness tests that run models with mixed evictions.

sam: I'll add the metrics and a small dashboard.

runtime-bot: Deploy notice: runtime-canary cluster will pick up commits from branch kv-page-interop tomorrow for early telem.

jess: thanks all. Let's reconvene after the spike. :+1:
